title: Japan Lowers Speed Limit on Residential Roads
paragraphs: From September 1, 2026, drivers in Japan have had to slow down on many of the country's narrow residential streets. Under a change to the country's traffic rules, the legal speed limit on these roads has been cut from 60 kilometers per hour to 30 kilometers per hour.

The new limit applies to residential roads that do not have a center line and do not have speed limit signs. According to reports, around 870,000 kilometers of road are affected, which is roughly 70% of Japan's general roads.

However, not every road has changed. Roads that already have speed limit signs will continue to follow the limits shown on the signs. For example, if a sign on a residential road says that the limit is 40 kilometers per hour, drivers may still drive at that speed. In addition, roads that have a center line, or where traffic going in different directions is physically separated, will keep the legal limit of 60 kilometers per hour unless signs say otherwise.

The main purpose of the change is to protect pedestrians, especially children and elderly people. Although the total number of traffic deaths in Japan has fallen to a record low, the number of accidents involving these vulnerable groups on residential roads has not gone down. Research shows that pedestrians are much less likely to die in an accident when cars are traveling at less than 30 kilometers per hour.
Japanese police have asked drivers to recognize that they need to take particular care on roads shared by cars, pedestrians and cyclists.

The penalties for breaking the new rule can be serious. Drivers caught going 60 kilometers per hour or faster on a road with the new 30 kilometer limit could face up to six months in prison or a fine of up to 100,000 yen.

Some people, however, have pointed out that many narrow streets in Japan already had a limit of 30 kilometers per hour. Others have noted that lowering the legal limit does not automatically mean that drivers will actually slow down.
